title: More data than the network can carry
teaches: Pipelines for instruments and fleets: filter at the source, upload or ship the disks, resumable chunked uploads, tiered storage, and a catalogue

parts.title: A petabyte a second, kept to a trickle

blocks.text: When the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, on the border of France and Switzerland, began colliding protons for physics in March 2010, its big detectors faced a problem no network could solve. The machine was built to cross bunches of protons up to 40 million times a second, and each crossing lights up millions of detector channels. Writing all of this data down would require a throughput of roughly 1 PB/s. Instead, the experiments filter the data at the source. A first **trigger**, built in custom hardware, inspects a coarse picture of each crossing within a few microseconds and keeps about 100,000 crossings a second. A farm of thousands of computers then reconstructs those events in more detail and writes about 1,000 crossings a second to disk. Roughly one crossing in 40,000 is ever saved.

Other fleets of instruments meet a smaller version of the same bottleneck. From 2007 Google's Street View cars drove the world's roads with rings of cameras, and later laser scanners, recording far more data than a car's mobile connection could transmit; the recordings returned on the cars' own hard drives. The computer scientist Andrew Tanenbaum had stated this principle in his textbook *Computer Networks*, noting that engineers should never underestimate the bandwidth of a station wagon full of tapes hurtling down the highway.[^wagon] In 2016 Amazon applied the same principle with Snowmobile, a shipping container on a lorry that carried 100 PB from a customer's datacentre to its own.

In this lesson, we will design a data ingestion pipeline for **1,000 survey vehicles**, each carrying cameras and laser scanners that record about **1 TB an hour**, driving **8 hours a day**. Engineers need anomalous events delivered within minutes, all retained data ingested within a day or two, and the ability to query specific scenarios across years of driving. We will design this pipeline and then compare it with the systems published by CERN, Amazon, Dropbox and Facebook.

parts.title: What it must do, and what it need not

blocks.text: **Functional.** We must transfer every byte worth keeping from the vehicles to the datacentre without losing any retained data. We must deliver small, urgent payloads (such as a system fault, a rare event flagged by an onboard detector, or vehicle telemetry) within minutes. We need to store the ingested data cheaply for as long as retention policies require, let engineers query segments by time, location and scene contents, and blur faces and number plates before anyone browses the imagery.

**Non-functional.** Retained data must have a durability of eleven nines a year (the standard figure advertised by commercial object stores, meaning a store of a billion objects loses about one object every hundred years).[^nines] Network transfer and storage costs must remain economical per vehicle, and a vehicle that goes offline for a week must not lose any recorded data.

**Out of scope.** We will not design the onboard recording software, the machine-learning detectors that tag scenes, or the downstream systems that consume the data, such as map-building pipelines or simulation testing (lesson D6). Each of those is a large system of its own. We will focus on the ingestion and storage pipeline that connects them, which accounts for the bulk of the infrastructure cost.
Before drawing any system diagrams, estimate how long a high-speed network link would take to transfer one day of driving data.

blocks.caption: Throughput estimates for a fleet that records more data than a network link can transfer.
blocks.task: Guess, then try a smaller fleet and a faster link

blocks.text: The fleet generates 8 PB of data a day. A 10 Gb/s link, which is a fast connection for a depot, transfers at most 108 TB a day. Uploading one day of driving over that link would take over ten weeks, and the backlog would grow by 7.9 PB every day. A vehicle's cellular connection at 50 Mb/s, running continuously while it drives, can transfer about 2% of what the sensors record, and metered cellular bandwidth is expensive. This arithmetic leaves us two levers, which you can test in the workbench below. First, we can reduce the data volume by filtering on the vehicle to keep only relevant segments, just as CERN's triggers do. Second, we can move the bulk data over the cheapest path with the highest bandwidth: physical hard drives carried by vehicles that return to the depot anyway.

On the vehicle, sensor data writes continuously into a **ring buffer** that holds the last 30 minutes of full-resolution data, overwriting older recordings as new ones arrive. Most of what passes through the buffer is uneventful driving on an empty road. **Triggers** mark time windows to keep at full resolution, such as a hard braking event, an operator pressing a button, an onboard detector spotting a rare object, or two sensors producing conflicting readings. Everything else is downsampled, summarised, or discarded. You can test different retention rates in the workbench below; reducing the kept volume by a factor of 25 (from 100% to 4%) reduces the load on every downstream network link and storage tier by the same factor of 25. Engineers calibrate trigger thresholds by also saving a small random sample of all driving, say 0.1% of minutes, regardless of trigger activity. Comparing the triggered segments against that uniform sample shows what the triggers miss. Engineers set triggers for rare events with loose thresholds so they fire too often rather than too rarely, because a false alarm only costs a few gigabytes of storage.

The kept data leaves the vehicle over one of two paths, depending on urgency. The **narrow pipe** is the cellular network, which carries minute-by-minute vehicle telemetry, a metadata index of recorded segments, small thumbnails of triggered events, and the raw sensor window for any urgent fault. Cellular links provide tens of megabits a second at most and cost dollars per gigabyte, so we reserve this path for small, high-priority payloads that must arrive within minutes. The **wide pipe** is the physical depot: when the vehicle returns to base each night, it uploads data over a fast local network, or technicians swap its removable drives for empty ones and ship the full drives to the datacentre by van. This path has a latency of hours to days, but the transfer cost per byte is nearly zero.

Some fleets require a third path, a **live link**, so a remote operator at a desk can view a machine's camera feeds and provide guidance when it requests help, such as a geologist steering a rover on a distant slope. The latency budget from camera lens to operator screen is tight: encoding a video frame takes 20 ms to 30 ms, the cellular uplink adds 50 ms to 100 ms under good conditions, a cloud relay adds 10 ms, and decoding and display take 20 ms, totalling under 250 ms at low resolution. Because cellular coverage drops out in patches, the vehicle transmits duplicate streams over two cellular carriers simultaneously and the receiver uses whichever packet arrives first.[^bond] Even with redundancy, the connection will sometimes fail, so engineers design the vehicle never to depend on the live link for safety. The remote operator provides high-level advice while the onboard computer executes control decisions, and a dropped link leaves the vehicle in a safe state that it can reach autonomously. In lesson 23, we call this property **static stability**, where a system continues operating safely without assistance from a failed dependency. The system logs every command and message so engineers can audit decisions after an incident.

Transferring a 256 GB log file over a depot's Wi-Fi network takes most of an hour, and wireless connections drop frequently. If an upload restarts from the beginning after every disconnection, it may never finish. To make uploads resumable, the vehicle splits the file into **chunks** of a few megabytes and names each chunk by the SHA-256 hash of its byte contents. When a vehicle reconnects, it sends the storage server the list of chunk hashes that make up the file; the server replies with the hashes it is missing, and the vehicle uploads only those chunks. A dropped connection wastes at most one chunk. Furthermore, the vehicle never uploads any chunk the store already holds, such as a standard calibration file carried by every vehicle, a shared map package, or a duplicate log copied from two drives. A storage system that identifies data by the cryptographic hash of its contents is called **content-addressed**.[^hash] Choosing the chunk size involves a trade-off: splitting a 256 GB log into 4 MB chunks produces 64,000 hashes (a 2 MB manifest), whereas 4 KB chunks would produce a 2 GB manifest, and 1 GB chunks would waste up to 1 GB on a dropped connection while finding fewer duplicate chunks across files. A chunk size of a few megabytes balances manifest overhead against retry cost.

blocks.caption: A log uploaded as a single file or in hash-named chunks over a link that drops once.
blocks.task: Upload in chunks, then move the Link drops at slider

blocks.text: Dropbox's desktop client uses this exact mechanism to synchronise files: it splits each file into 4 MB blocks, hashes each block with SHA-256, and uploads only the blocks the server lacks. Editing one page of a large document transfers only the modified blocks, and a popular file stored by thousands of users is written to disk only once. A complete **file sync** service combines this content-addressed block store with a metadata database of file versions (where each version is an ordered list of block hashes) and a change journal that clients poll or subscribe to for updates. When two users edit the same file while offline, the server retains both versions and saves the second upload as a "conflicted copy", because automatically merging arbitrary binary file formats is impossible in general (lesson 13 showed the complexity required just to merge plain text).

Inside the datacentre, the pipeline stores chunks in an object store. The object store separates its **metadata** (the index of which objects exist and which storage nodes hold their bytes) from the raw data payloads, just as the Google File System separated its master server from its chunkservers (lesson 6). It also accepts large files via **multipart upload**, allowing clients to upload chunks in parallel and in any order, concatenating them into a single logical object only when the final chunk arrives. Directory listings and catalogue queries read only the metadata index; the system never reads the bulk storage disks until an engineer requests the underlying sensor bytes.

You can now configure the pipeline's main parameters: the percentage of data each vehicle retains after onboard triage, the transport path for bulk data, and whether segments older than 30 days migrate to cold storage. The model uses representative unit costs: $60 per TB per month for hot storage replicated across three copies, $4 per TB per month for cold storage using erasure coding (which splits data into fragments plus redundant parity fragments so any sufficient subset can reconstruct the original, as covered in lesson 7), and $1 per GB for cellular bandwidth. The fleet operates out of ten depots, each equipped with a 10 Gb/s network link, or vans that ship physical drives once a day from each depot.

blocks.caption: One year of operation for a 1,000-vehicle fleet. The link labels show daily throughput on each path, and the monthly bill totals the ongoing transport cost plus the storage cost after one year of accumulation.
blocks.task: Keep up with the fleet, with old data in cold storage, for under $3 million a month

blocks.text: Retaining 100% of the recordings overwhelms every transport path: 8 PB a day exceeds the ten depots' combined network capacity of 1.08 PB a day, and shipping physical drives would accumulate nearly 3 EB of storage a year. Filtering the data on the vehicles down to 4% reduces the daily volume to 320 TB, which the ten depots' combined 100 Gb/s links can upload in about seven hours overnight. Over a year, the fleet accumulates about 117 PB of data. Keeping all 117 PB in three-way replicated hot storage costs about $7 million a month; keeping only the most recent 30 days hot and migrating older data to erasure-coded cold storage drops the storage bill to about $1 million a month. The cellular path has low bandwidth and the highest cost per byte, so we reserve it for urgent payloads that cannot wait until the vehicle reaches a depot.

**Retention** policy is our third cost and compliance lever, often dictated by privacy regulations. Raw camera imagery from public streets contains human faces and vehicle licence plates. A standard ingestion pipeline runs automated blurring models on arrival, retains the unblurred raw footage only briefly to verify detector and blurring accuracy, and stores the derived data (such as object tags, trajectories, and blurred video) for much longer. Engineers must also design for targeted deletion: when a member of the public requests the removal of their personal data, the system must locate and purge every relevant segment across all storage tiers, which is another reason we need an accurate metadata catalogue.

**Handling a week-long depot network outage.** If a depot's network link goes down for a week, the vehicles' onboard drives will begin to fill up. We must design a priority queue for uploads in advance: the depot network uploads triggered event windows before routine background samples, ensuring that a prolonged outage leaves only the least valuable data waiting in the backlog, or prompts technicians to ship the physical drives by van. The ingestion pipeline is idempotent, as described in lesson 22: because chunks are content-addressed, uploading a chunk twice over Wi-Fi or reading the same chunk from a shipped drive writes no duplicate data to the store.

A 117 PB object store that engineers cannot search is useless for development. Engineers need to run queries like "find every night-time minute with a cyclist near a junction" to test a new perception model, build a machine-learning training set, or measure how often a rare scenario occurs in the real world. Scanning every raw log file to answer that query would require reading all 117 PB from disk.

blocks.caption: One year of retained one-minute driving segments, tagged with approximate occurrence rates: night 30%, junction 20%, rain 10%, cyclist 5%, and roadworks 3%.
blocks.task: Ask the catalogue for two things at once

blocks.text: To avoid full scans, the pipeline writes a **catalogue** at ingest time: a relational or key-value database that stores metadata about the recordings forever. Each row represents a one-minute segment and records the vehicle ID, the start and end timestamps, the geographic map cells the vehicle traversed (lesson M2), the onboard software and sensor calibration versions, the object store pointers for its chunks, and scene tags generated by batch detector jobs that run over newly ingested logs (lesson 8). Because the catalogue indexes segments by time, map cell, and tag using an inverted index like a search engine (lesson D3), it can answer a query for `night AND cyclist AND junction` by intersecting three posting lists in milliseconds. The system then fetches only the matching segments from the object store: assuming the tags in the figure are statistically independent, that query reads about 0.35 PB instead of 117 PB.

Maintaining a catalogue enables two additional workflows. First, a machine-learning **dataset** becomes a saved query result frozen as an immutable list of segment IDs and data versions, guaranteeing that an evaluation job run months later reads the exact same sensor bytes (lesson D6). Second, **change detection** becomes a database query: segments where the vehicle's live perception disagrees with the current high-definition map (such as a newly built roundabout or a closed lane) generate proposed map edits. Engineers or automated checks verify and merge these proposals into a new map version, which then rolls out to the fleet in stages like any other software release (lessons M1 and D7).

CERN's data pipeline represents source filtering at an extreme scale: hardware and software triggers discard all but one proton bunch crossing in 40,000 before writing anything to disk. The retained data, amounting to tens of petabytes a year, replicates outward from CERN across a tiered global computing grid, where national datacentres store archival copies and university clusters run physics analyses.[^grid] As our workbench model showed, filtering data at the source reduces the capacity required at every downstream stage.

Amazon's Snowball storage appliances and Snowmobile container lorry package the physical wide pipe as a commercial service for datacentre migrations where network uploads would take months. Dropbox's client sync protocol pioneered chunked, content-addressed uploads at consumer scale; in 2016, Dropbox also migrated its underlying block storage off Amazon S3 into its own custom object store, Magic Pocket, which uses erasure coding across datacentres to reduce storage costs. Similarly, Facebook's f4 storage system, published in 2014, implemented hot-and-cold storage tiering for user photos: newly uploaded photos reside in a Haystack store with three full replicas to serve high read traffic, while older photos with lower request rates migrate to an erasure-coded warm store, reducing the effective storage overhead from 3.6x the raw photo size to 2.1x.[^f4]

Onboard triggers, two transport pipes, and chunked uploads solve the bandwidth and storage capacity constraints, while the metadata catalogue lets engineers query specific driving scenarios without scanning petabytes of raw files.

parts.title: At ten and a hundred times

blocks.text: **Scaling to 10,000 vehicles** requires ten times as many depots and network links, which scales horizontally by adding identical infrastructure. However, the object store now grows by more than 1 EB a year, making cold storage capacity the single largest operational expense rather than network transfer. At this scale, engineering and finance teams must tighten retention policies and lower the onboard trigger rates to keep storage growth affordable.

**Scaling to 100,000 vehicles** requires moving computation out to the depots where the data arrives. Instead of uploading all retained raw logs to a central cloud region, local server racks at each depot run the batch perception detectors and privacy blurring overnight. The depots then upload only the generated tags, summary statistics, and the specific raw sensor windows that engineers have explicitly requested, much as CERN places its high-level trigger farm directly beside the particle detector. The central catalogue becomes the largest database in the architecture, structured as a distributed sorted table keyed by `(cell, time)` in the style of Bigtable (lesson 10), while the depots overwrite unrequested raw data as soon as their local disks fill.

blocks.caption: Seven questions on moving and keeping a fleet's data
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A fleet records 8 PB a day and each of its ten depots has a 10 Gb/s link moving about 108 TB a day. Which plan is realistic?
choices: Upgrade every depot to 100 Gb/s and keep it all
Triage on board and upload only the few per cent worth keeping
Upload everything over cellular while driving, so that nothing waits for the depot at night
items.why: Ten 100 Gb/s links could barely transfer 8 PB a day, and the central object store would then grow by nearly 3 EB a year; cellular links can carry only about 2% of the data. Filtering on the vehicle reduces the load on every network link and storage tier downstream.

items.ask: Why do instrument pipelines such as the LHC's decide what to keep at the source?
choices: Because data filtered later can't be compressed as well as the raw data that comes from the sensors
Because the source has the most accurate clock, so only the source can put the events in order
Because every byte dropped there is a byte that no link, disk or later stage has to pay for
items.why: Any volume reduction achieved at the source reduces the capacity needed at every downstream network link and storage system. CERN's triggers save roughly one bunch crossing in 40,000.

items.ask: A 256 GB upload is split into 4 MB chunks named by SHA-256 hashes. The link drops at 60%. What happens on reconnecting?
choices: The vehicle sends the list of hashes, the store names those it lacks, and only they are sent
The upload restarts, but faster, because the store has cached the chunks it saw the first time
The store waits for the vehicle to resend the whole file, then compares the two copies
items.why: A dropped connection wastes at most the single chunk in flight, and chunks the object store already holds are never uploaded again.

items.ask: A live link lets a person at a desk guide a machine in the field. What must happen when the link drops?
choices: It stops in place and waits, however long the link is down
The machine goes on with whatever command it last received, for as long as the link is down
It brings itself to a safe state on its own, without waiting for the link
items.why: Cellular links fail unpredictably. Because the remote operator only advises while the onboard computer executes control, the machine must be able to reach a safe state autonomously when the connection drops.

items.ask: After a year, 117 PB are stored. Keeping all of it in three hot copies costs about $7 million a month. What cuts the bill most?
choices: Compressing every segment again each month with a stronger and slower codec
Keeping the last 30 days hot and moving older data to erasure-coded cold storage
Storing two copies instead of three in the hot store, accepting a lower durability
items.why: Engineers read older data much less frequently than recent logs. Erasure coding stores cold data with far less storage overhead than the 3x multiplier of three-way replication, using dense, inexpensive disks.

items.ask: Engineers want every night-time minute with a cyclist near a junction from a year of logs. What makes that fast?
choices: A catalogue written at ingest, indexed by time, place and tag, so only the matching segments are ever read
A larger cluster that reads all of the logs in parallel, so that the whole scan finishes overnight
Storing the logs in date order, so that the year's night-time minutes sit next to one another on disk
items.why: Without a metadata catalogue, a query must scan every byte in the object store. With an indexed catalogue, the database intersects the tag lists in milliseconds and reads only the matching segments from storage.

items.ask: In a file sync service, how is a file's new version stored after a small edit?
choices: As a full new copy, so that each version can be read without reference to any other version
As a list of block hashes, most of them shared with the old version
As a diff against the previous version
items.why: Unmodified 4 MB blocks keep the same SHA-256 hashes, so an edit uploads and stores only the specific blocks that changed.

summary: **Calculate bandwidth before choosing a network link.** A fleet of 1,000 vehicles recording 1 TB an hour generates 8 PB a day, which would take over ten weeks to upload over a single 10 Gb/s link.
**Filter data at the source.** Using an onboard ring buffer and event triggers reduces the load on every downstream network link and storage tier by the same factor.

**Use two transport pipes based on urgency.** Send small, urgent telemetry and fault logs over cellular links within minutes, and move the bulk recordings via depot networks or shipped drives over hours or days.

**Design machines so the live link is optional.** Budget end-to-end latency under 250 ms, transmit over two cellular carriers simultaneously, and ensure the vehicle transitions to a safe state autonomously when the link drops.
**Upload files in content-addressed chunks.** Naming 4 MB chunks by their SHA-256 hash ensures a dropped link wastes at most one chunk, and chunks the store already holds are never uploaded again.

**Separate metadata from raw sensor bytes.** Keep the object store's chunk index and the segment catalogue in fast databases, reading the bulk storage disks only when an engineer fetches specific recordings.

**Tier storage by age and access frequency.** Keep recent recordings hot in three-way replicated storage, migrate data older than 30 days to erasure-coded cold storage, and enforce automated deletion policies for privacy compliance.

**Populate a searchable catalogue at ingest.** Indexing segments by timestamp, map cell, and scene tag turns petabyte-scale log scans into millisecond index lookups, enabling reproducible training datasets and map change detection.

wagon.title: The station wagon
wagon.text: Tanenbaum's line appears in his textbook *Computer Networks*, first published in 1981. The arithmetic still holds: a van carrying a thousand 20 TB drives on a six-hour journey moves 20 PB, achieving an effective throughput of about 7.4 Tb/s, which exceeds most datacentres' external network links.

nines.title: Eleven nines
nines.text: An annual durability of 99.999999999% means each stored object has a one in 100 billion probability of being lost in a given year. Object stores achieve this by distributing replicas or erasure-coded fragments across independent failure domains and reconstructing lost fragments quickly when disks fail (lesson 7). This figure is a probabilistic model estimate; in practice, software bugs and operator mistakes cause most data loss.

bond.title: Two carriers at once
bond.text: Transmitting every packet over two cellular networks simultaneously and keeping whichever copy arrives first doubles the bandwidth cost but sharply reduces packet loss. If each carrier drops packets 2% of the time independently, both carriers fail at the same moment only 0.04% of the time. This technique applies the hedged requests of lesson 9 to wireless links.

hash.title: Naming by hash
hash.text: The probability that two different data chunks produce the same 256-bit SHA-256 hash is so small that storage systems safely use the hash as a unique identifier. The server also computes the SHA-256 hash of every chunk it receives and compares it against the chunk's name, immediately detecting and rejecting any bytes corrupted in transit.

grid.title: The grid
grid.text: The Worldwide LHC Computing Grid consists of a Tier 0 facility at CERN that stores the primary copy of the filtered raw data, roughly a dozen large Tier 1 national centres around the world that hold secondary replicas and run batch reprocessing, and over a hundred Tier 2 centres, mostly at universities, that run Monte Carlo simulations and end-user physics analyses.

f4.title: Warm storage
f4.text: Facebook's Haystack storage system kept newly uploaded photos in three full replicas (plus geographic backups, totalling 3.6x overhead) to serve high request rates. Its 2014 f4 paper showed that request rates for photos drop sharply after the first few weeks, and described migrating older photos to Reed-Solomon erasure-coded storage within and across datacentres, reducing the storage footprint from 3.6 bytes per byte of photo to 2.1 bytes.
